cards.explanation: The answer is to be cursed and cut off from Christ. Paul, the apostle writing this letter, says, “…I could wish that I myself were cursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers…” That's how much his heart hurts for them. I've never cared about anybody enough to wish that, and I once gave up the last cookie in the box for a neighbor and cried about it.

The answer is Israel. Paul calls his brothers “…the people of Israel.” in verse 4, and he says they're his own flesh and blood. He's writing about his own family here, friends. I think that's why his sorrow runs so deep.

The answer is True. Paul says “…from them proceeds the human descent of Christ, who is God over all, forever worthy of praise! Amen.” He doesn't just stop at the family tree, bakers. He ends it with praise, and I think that tells you how he feels about Christ.

The answer is that not all who are descended from Israel are Israel. Paul says, “…not all who are descended from Israel are Israel.” God's word hasn't fallen apart, friends. Paul is saying the people it speaks of aren't simply everyone born into the family line.

The answer is Isaac. Paul quotes, “Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned.” Isaac was Abraham's son. Paul is showing, friends, that the promise runs through one particular son, not just any son.

The answer is False. Paul says it is not the children of the flesh who are God's children, but “…it is the children of the promise who are regarded as offspring.” So the children of the promise are the ones regarded as offspring, bakers. You can't just be born into this one. It runs on the promise.

The answer is Sarah. The promise says, “At the appointed time I will return, and Sarah will have a son.” Sarah was Abraham's wife (Genesis 11:29). The promise came first, friends, and then came Isaac.
The answer is False. Paul says it was “…before the twins were born or had done anything good or bad…” Nobody had earned anything yet, bakers. Paul says it's “…not by works but by Him who calls…”

The answer is that the older will serve the younger. Rebecca was told, “The older will serve the younger.” Paul says it came “…not by works but by Him who calls…” Verse 11 adds, friends, that this was said before the twins were born or had done anything good or bad.

The answer is Jacob. The line says, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” It's a heavy line, and I think it's worth reading slowly. Paul has just said, friends, that this was settled before the twins were born or had done anything good or bad.
The answer is Certainly not. Paul asks, “Is God unjust?” and answers right away, “Certainly not!” He doesn't hedge or add an exception, friends. The next verses are where he explains.

The answer is that He'll have mercy on whom He has mercy. Paul says God told Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.” Mercy belongs to God to give, bakers. Nobody can order it up like a tray of cookies.
The answer is mercy. Paul says, “So then, it does not depend on man’s desire or effort, but on God’s mercy.” You can't bake your way into it with extra effort, friends. It's a gift.

The answer is power. The Scripture says to Pharaoh, “I raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power in you…” Pharaoh was the king of Egypt in Moses' day (Exodus 6:11). Power is the purpose God names there, bakers.

The answer is False. The Scripture says to Pharaoh, “…that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth.” All the earth is much bigger than Egypt, friends. And it's the same verse that talks about power.

The answer is why God still finds fault. Paul says someone will ask, “Then why does God still find fault? For who can resist His will?” He puts the pushback right on the table, bakers. Then he answers it.

The answer is True. Paul asks, “Shall what is formed say to Him who formed it…” and then gives the words the formed thing would say. It's a picture of the made talking back to the maker, friends. He sets that picture right after the question in verse 19.

The answer is a special vessel and a common one. Paul says the potter can make “…one vessel for special occasions and another for common use?” Both come from the same lump of clay, bakers. It's a picture of the potter's right.

The answer is with great patience. Paul says God, intending to show His wrath and make His power known, “…bore with great patience the vessels of His wrath, prepared for destruction?” Then the sentence keeps going in verse 23: “What if He did this to make the riches of His glory known to the vessels of His mercy…” So Paul doesn't stop at wrath, friends. He goes on to the riches of God's glory and the vessels of His mercy.

The answer is called. Paul says the vessels of mercy include us, “…whom He has called not only from the Jews, but also from the Gentiles?” Gentiles are people who aren't Jewish, friends. So the calling reaches both.
The answer is My People. God says in Hosea, “I will call them ‘My People’ who are not My people…” Hosea was a prophet (Hosea 1:1-2). People once called not His own, bakers, get a new name from Him.

The answer is True. Paul quotes, “It will happen that in the very place where it was said to them, ‘You are not My people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’…” The same place where they heard no gets a new answer, friends. That's the promise Paul brings from Hosea.

The answer is only the remnant. Isaiah says, “Though the number of the Israelites is like the sand of the sea, only the remnant will be saved.” The number is huge, bakers, but the remnant is who's named.

The answer is False. Isaiah says, “For the Lord will carry out His sentence on the earth thoroughly and decisively.” Thoroughly and decisively, friends, not slowly and not halfway. Paul passes along Isaiah's words in verse 28.

The answer is Sodom and Gomorrah. Isaiah says, “Unless the Lord of Hosts had left us descendants, we would have become like Sodom, we would have resembled Gomorrah.” The descendants left to them make the difference, bakers. Paul says it's just as Isaiah foretold.
